opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing for us was that we really wanted to measure the model, not the scaffolding. There are a lot of agent frameworks out there that do impressive things, but many of them add a lot of hand-engineered structure: planning steps, specialized retrieval, multiple sub-agents checking each other. Those can push benchmark numbers up, but then it's hard to tell how much is the model and how much is clever prompt engineering around it.

So our philosophy was to give as much control as possible to the model itself. Keep the harness really simple: a prompt, a way to run bash commands, and a way to view and edit files. Then let the model decide how to explore the repo, when to write a reproduction script, when to run tests, and when it's done. SWE-agent was close to that spirit. It's a well-understood, fairly lightweight setup the community already knew, so results are comparable and people can reproduce them.

Honestly, a lot of the work wasn't in the framework at all. It was in the tool design. We spent a surprising amount of time on things like the file-editing tool: what format the model uses to specify edits, how errors get reported back, requiring absolute paths so it doesn't get confused after changing directories. I think of it like designing a good interface for a human engineer. If you'd give a junior developer clear docs and a sane interface, you should do the same for the model. Those small details made a much bigger difference than any fancy orchestration.

And the other reason is forward-looking. As models get better, heavy scaffolding tends to become a crutch, or even gets in the way. A minimal setup lets you see the gains from a better model directly. You're not fighting against assumptions baked into the framework from when models were weaker.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-agent was familiar, lightweight, and supported comparable, reproducible results, but does not mention shared authorship with SWE-bench as a reason for choosing it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, we didn't start out wanting to build a framework. When we were putting together our SWE-bench Verified submission, we looked at what was already out there, and SWE-agent was the most mature, best-understood scaffold at the time. The team at Princeton had done a lot of careful work on the agent-computer interface: how you present files to the model, how you handle edits, how you give it a sane set of commands instead of just dumping it into a raw shell. Starting from that meant we weren't reinventing things that had already been figured out, and it also meant our results were comparable to other people's. If we'd built some bespoke system from scratch, nobody would know whether the gains came from the model or from the scaffold.

That said, we ended up stripping it down quite a bit. A lot of what SWE-agent does is compensate for weaknesses in earlier models, and with Claude 3.5 Sonnet we found the model did better with less hand-holding. We gave it a very minimal set of tools, essentially a bash tool and an edit tool, let it see the full error output instead of truncated summaries, and prompted it to think more and take its time. So we used SWE-agent as a starting point and a sanity check, but the lesson for us was that as models get stronger, the scaffold should get simpler and get out of the way.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-agent was mature and using it made results comparable, but it does not say SWE-agent and SWE-bench shared authorship or that this made the framework choice seem neutral.

astra-6.text: We wanted to start with a framework built specifically for software engineering, rather than build all the scaffolding ourselves. The interesting part for us was how the agent would approach the task—how it would explore the code, make a change, and test it. SWE-agent gave us a starting point for that loop, so we could focus on the agent’s behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-agent was purpose-built for software engineering and provided a starting point for the task loop. It does not mention shared authorship with SWE-bench or present that as a reason for choosing a neutral framework.

sol-6.1.text: The appeal was that SWE-agent already had the basic loop we wanted: the model can inspect a repository, run commands, make changes, and look at the results. That meant we could focus on the agent’s behavior instead of building all of that infrastructure ourselves. And it was relatively straightforward to understand and modify, which matters when you’re experimenting—you want to be able to tell why something worked or why it failed.
